title: Decoding the Right-to-Repair Debate
text:
Decoding the Right-to-Repair Debate

Photo: NAVCENT Public Affairs/DVIDS

Critical Questions
by

Jerry McGinn,

Patrick Armstrong ,
and
Alek Jovovic

Published October 28, 2026

This is the second article in the CSIS Center for the Industrial Base series on the right to repair. For additional background, see the previous piece.

The “right to repair” has emerged as one of the most contentious issues in present-day U.S. defense acquisition policy. At the center of the debate is a simple question: Who should control the technical data and intellectual property needed to maintain and repair U.S. military equipment? As Congress works to achieve consensus on this issue in the FY 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), it is increasingly important for lawmakers, industry, and the public to understand the nuances of the right-to-repair debate and the legal frameworks that underpin it.Q1: What is the right to repair?A1: Before the U.S. Department of Defense (DOD) signs a contract with an industry contractor for new equipment or weapons systems, both parties must negotiate control over the technical data and software rights associated with these products. When the government funds the development of a system, it generally is entitled to broad intellectual property (IP) rights. Absent that funding, original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) typically retain significant control of their product’s IP. While this partnership has varied over time, the DOD has relied on OEMs to conduct significant maintenance, repair, and sustainment of its weapons and equipment. However, prominent voices in the DOD and Congress are now calling for greater government control over the technical data necessary to perform maintenance. This push has created growing tension among industry, Congress, and the DOD over the future of IP rights, culminating in a debate over the right to repair.Q2: How do IP rights affect the industrial base?A2: For OEMs, control over technical data and IP helps preserve their competitive technical edge. It also enables them to generate long-term revenue by performing maintenance and repairs on government-owned systems that they manufactured.For the DOD, greater IP rights enable the government to pursue repair options independent of the OEM, either through in-house “organic” repairs performed by government personnel in government-owned facilities or through third-party industry providers. These options can be more affordable and efficient than relying on the OEM. As government officials emphasize, a reduced reliance on OEMs can be especially significant when repairs must be executed in the field, far from OEM repair facilities and personnel.Q3: What is the status of right-to-repair legislation in Congress?A3: As the right to repair has become an increasingly salient issue, the debate has culminated in a congressional battle over provisions in the annual NDAA for the past two years. For the FY 2026 NDAA, lawmakers enacted Section 805, a measure mandating that the DOD identify deficiencies and gaps in its control of technical data rights for military systems. This was a necessary first step in identifying IP deficiencies and their impact on readiness, but lawmakers are eager to incorporate a more comprehensive solution into the FY 2027 NDAA.The House and Senate have each created their own version of the FY 2027 NDAA, each featuring a right-to-repair amendment. The House bill shifts the burden of proof onto contractors, requiring industry to justify its right to retain tighter IP control in government contracts. The Senate bill goes a step further by making government IP access a precondition of doing business with the DOD. Reconciling these two bills will require formal negotiation between the two chambers once both distinct bills are finalized.While the House has passed its version of the NDAA, the Senate has yet to bring its version to the floor, and with both chambers now in recess for the midterm elections, no further action is expected until Congress returns.Q4: What are government purpose rights, and why do they matter?A4: Government purpose rights (GPR) are at the center of the current right-to-repair debate and are a core concept in government contracting. Put simply, GPR gives the government the right to use, modify, and share IP freely within the government, and to release it to third parties, provided it is used solely for “government purposes.” More restrictive frameworks for IP rights include limited rights and restricted rights, which bar the government from releasing IP to third parties or using it for manufacturing without the contractor’s consent. By contrast, an unlimited rights framework grants the government virtually unrestricted ability to use and release commercial IP (it is important to note that GPR typically converts to unlimited rights five years after the initial contract). Finally, specifically negotiated license rights allow negotiators to craft bespoke IP agreements, often threading the needle between GPR and limited rights.Traditionally, the level of IP control granted to the government in DOD contracts varies from case to case, often depending on the degree of partnership between industry and government in the initial product development.However, a House amendment, put forth by Representatives Maggie Goodlander (D-NH) and Pat Harrigan (R-NC), would make GPR the default IP rights framework in DOD contracts. This amendment would place the responsibility on industry to demonstrate the need for more restrictive IP rights, paving the way for more government control over equipment maintenance, production, and alternative sources. Importantly, this change would apply only to future contracts, leaving the IP terms negotiated under agreements for existing equipment untouched.Q5: How would a GPR default change the federal procurement system?A5: From a government perspective, standardizing the use of GPR could significantly reduce repair costs and improve maintenance efficiency. As cited in previous CSIS analysis, sustainment accounts for roughly 70 percent of the total cost of major weapons systems and platforms. This default would therefore enable the DOD to perform in-house repairs or choose from multiple industry vendors, creating lower-cost repair alternatives to OEMs. To highlight this trade-off, Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) recently noted that a helicopter control knob, which cost the Army $47,000 to outsource for repair, could have been manufactured in-house for just $15. It is not clear, however, that GPR would be required for this repair.It is also important to note that a GPR default would raise contract prices significantly. Contractors would likely charge the government higher up-front prices to offset the loss of control over their IP and the future sustainment revenue they would otherwise earn by performing repairs.From an industry perspective, the most controversial element of default GPR is the government’s ability to share privately developed contractor IP with third parties. Industry stakeholders argue that the Goodlander-Harrigan amendment would prevent contractors from protecting their technical data from potential competitors, creating an uneven playing field across the industrial base.Q6: What is the distinction between maintenance and manufacturing data?A6: Much like the different types of IP rights, grasping the distinction between the two forms of technical data—operation, maintenance, installation, and training data (OMIT), and detailed manufacturing and process data (DMPD)—is crucial for understanding the right-to-repair debate. Simply put, OMIT data enables the government to operate and maintain equipment and weapons systems, while DMPD provides instructions necessary for manufacturing and overhauling these assets. Under current U.S. law, industry is required to grant the government unlimited rights to OMIT data in procurement contracts. By contrast, control over DMPD varies with the level of government investment during product development.However, there is a degree of overlap between OMIT data and DMPD, creating a major source of tension in the right-to-repair debate. DOD guidelines acknowledge that some OMIT data also qualifies as DMPD and state that this data does not automatically fall under unlimited rights like the rest of OMIT. This overlap has led to high-profile disagreements between the government and industry on what technical data the government can access. As a result, a central question in the debate over any right-to-repair legislation will be how it applies to DMPD.Q7: How does the government manage and track IP rights?A7: While acquiring IP rights is a fundamental issue behind the right to repair, the government’s ability to track the rights it already owns is just as important. Effectively identifying, locating, and accessing existing IP enables the government to determine whether to buy new data or draw on preexisting IP knowledge. A recent Government Accountability Office report found that the DOD has consistently failed to acquire and track the IP and technical data rights necessary to sustain its equipment and weapons systems. The failure to plan for long-term product use and a lack of department-wide coordination were identified as key factors contributing to this issue. This fragmented approach also creates challenges for industry, as inadequate IP records limit the government’s ability to clearly define its technical data needs in negotiations, thereby limiting industry’s ability to offer an optimal proposal.Lawmakers added Section 805 to the FY 2026 NDAA to remedy this problem, mandating that the DOD identify and track the technical data and software it needs to maintain the military’s major weapons systems and address any gaps in its access to these rights. The DOD’s response to Section 805 was to create a database cataloging its existing IP and data access. However, at the time of writing, many industry stakeholders and lawmakers remain frustrated with the DOD’s apparent lack of progress on this database. Additionally, some observers have raised concerns in discussion with the authors about the potential security risks posed by a large, centralized database housing U.S. defense IP.Q8: What is the primary alternative to a GPR default?A8: Both the current case-by-case IP rights process and the proposed process outlined in the Goodlander-Harrigan amendment use an up-front payment model, in which the government pays for technical data rights at the outset of a contract. Industry, government, and members of Congress have proposed another framework, dubbed data as a service (DaaS). In this process, the government would pay a recurring subscription fee based on its usage of industry IP. Industry stakeholders highlight that this plan would streamline the acquisition process and create a more flexible approach to IP usage. Critics, however, claim that such a plan would unfairly burden taxpayers and create operational risks by denying the government the controls it needs to use IP effectively.Q9: What solutions could help resolve the right-to-repair debate?A9: The FY 2026 NDAA compromise did not satisfy anyone, and many lawmakers have made it clear that they are not willing to defer this issue further. Several pathways outlined below may help resolve the right-to-repair debate by addressing the concerns of both industry and government.One option is to make GPR the default mechanism for government contracts while barring the government from transferring the IP to third parties. This solution would address a key industry concern while allowing the DOD to use IP for organic repair. However, the cost of GPR would remain an issue.DaaS, explained above, is also a potential solution, allowing the government to gain IP access through recurring fees, much like a subscription. Additionally, some stakeholders have proposed in discussions with the authors a new business model for the DOD where the government would be responsible for switching vendors at various key points in a system’s life cycle. The DOD could therefore rely on one vendor for production and another for sustainment, and it would prepare for this switch by securing the appropriate IP rights during contract negotiations.Another potential solution would be to better delineate the distinction between OMIT data and DMPD. Many industry stakeholders highlight that sensitive software IP, such as source code, should be treated as DMPD and therefore be excluded from the unlimited rights framework for OMIT data. Therefore, the government, which already procures software using a dedicated process, could also develop a separate IP policy for software, distinct from a technical data policy. Similarly, the government could further customize its IP approach to accommodate different types of defense hardware, as munitions and missiles, for example, have significantly different technical data requirements and sustainment needs from ships and vehicles.Additional IP management frameworks, such as escrow and access agreements, also strike a balance between government and industry goals. In escrow agreements, a neutral third party ensures that IP is handed over to the government if the contractor files for bankruptcy or discontinues product support. Access agreements set specific conditions for government IP access, specifying who can access private technical data and where they can do so, often featuring nondisclosure agreements covering any data the government releases to outside contractors.Any effective solution to the right-to-repair issue will need to grapple with differing interpretations of the challenges, complex trade-offs, trailing outcomes, and competing interests discussed in this article. A follow-on article will further examine the potential solutions briefly outlined above.Jerry McGinn is director of the Center for the Industrial Base and a senior fellow with the Defense and Security Department at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) in Washington, D.C. Patrick Armstrong is a research intern in the Center for the Industrial Base at CSIS. Alek Jovovic is deputy director for the Center for the Industrial Base and senior fellow in the Defense and Security Department at CSIS.
